subject: Biology
title: Mass Extinctions: Evolution's Reset Button
description: Learn Mass Extinctions: Evolution's Reset Button in one minute.

hook.text: Life on Earth has nearly been wiped out five times. Each time, the survivors reinvented the world.

buildup.text: The Permian extinction killed 96% of marine species. The Cretaceous extinction ended the dinosaurs.

discovery.text: After each mass extinction, surviving lineages radiated into empty niches, creating entirely new ecosystems.

twist.text: Without the dinosaur extinction, mammals might still be shrew-sized nocturnal creatures today.

climax.text: Many scientists argue we're in a sixth mass extinction right now—caused by human activity.

punchline.text: Destruction clears the stage. Evolution writes a new play.

quiz.question: What percentage of marine species died in the Permian extinction?

details.summary: Mass extinctions have eliminated over 75 percent of species in geologically brief periods at least five times in Earth's history. While devastating, these events cleared ecological space for surviving lineages to diversify, from mammals after the dinosaur extinction to modern fauna.
details.whyItMatters: Mass extinctions reshape the trajectory of life on Earth. Many scientists argue we are now causing a sixth mass extinction through habitat destruction, pollution, and climate change, making this history urgently relevant.
takeaways: The Big Five mass extinctions each eliminated over 75 percent of species
The asteroid impact 66 million years ago ended the age of dinosaurs
Recovery from mass extinction typically takes 5 to 10 million years

faq.question: What caused the five major mass extinctions?
faq.answer: Causes vary. The end-Permian, the worst, involved massive volcanism and ocean chemistry changes. The K-Pg event was an asteroid impact. Others involved glaciation, ocean anoxia, or volcanic activity. Each had unique triggers but similar devastating outcomes.

faq.question: Are we currently in a sixth mass extinction?
faq.answer: Many scientists believe so. Current extinction rates are 100 to 1,000 times higher than background rates. Unlike past events caused by asteroids or volcanism, this one is driven by a single species through habitat destruction, overexploitation, pollution, and climate change.
